human_tolerance.notes: The article records that Cape porcupines 'are often considered pests by local farmers, because they can feed on crops and damage trees', which implies they readily work in ground that people have cleared and planted.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: A pair shares and jointly defends its territory and may occupy up to six burrows; the source describes no seasonal change in activity, so the phase spans the year.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's backbone accepts the trinomial Hystrix africaeaustralis at rank species and no longer matches the two-part Hystrix africaea, so that is the name used here.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 333530815 from the species/backbone endpoint. The iNaturalist taxon 44173 carries the same trinomial Hystrix africaea australis, matching GBIF. No Wikidata id is recorded: the English article carries no taxobox for this species.

conservation.note: The article carries a range map and describes a widely distributed, common and pest-tolerant species but does not print an IUCN category in its text, and there is no Wikidata item to carry one. LC is recorded as a judgement about a widespread southern African rodent; a reviewer should replace it with a sourced category.

range.note: The article carries a range map covering southern Africa but no written country list, so only ZA is recorded rather than inventing a country set. The Koppen classes cover the dry interior and the Cape winter-rainfall zone, and the elevation bracket is authored for a southern African terrestrial rodent.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walk is clear from a terrestrial rodent that forages on the ground. Burrow follows from 'Each pair may inhabit up to six burrows', which is where the pair shelters and breeds; the article does not describe the digging itself, so no separate digging gait is claimed.

traits.nest_type.note: Breeds in burrows: 'Gestation lasts around 94 days, and results in the birth of a litter of up to three young', in a pair's shared burrow.

traits.perching.note: A terrestrial rodent that forages on the ground and shelters in burrows; the article describes no climbing or perching.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the sourced 10 to 24 kg range, rounded to 17 kg. The article also records exceptionally large specimens at up to 30 kg and notes that in the Zimbabwe sample the female mean (18.4 kg) exceeded the male mean (16.9 kg).

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'They weigh from 10 to 24 kg', used directly.

traits.length_m.note: The schema wants nose to tail tip. The article gives 63 to 81 cm from head to base of tail and a further 11 to 20 cm of tail, so the combined range is 74 to 101 cm and its midpoint, 0.875 m, is recorded.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Relative to most other rodents, Cape porcupines are long-lived, surviving for 10 years in the wild, or up to 20 years in captivity.' The wild figure is used.

traits.home_range_ha.note: 'The size of the home range ... can range between at least 67 and 203 ha.' The midpoint, 135 ha, is recorded.

traits.diet.note: 'Cape porcupines eat mostly plant material: fruits, roots, tubers, bulbs, and bark ... They have also been reported to gnaw on carrion and bones.' The four-way split is authored: roots, tubers and bulbs are grouped under graze because the resource tag set has no root or tuber tag, and the 0.15 carrion share reflects 'have also been reported' rather than a routine part of the diet. The source gives no proportions.

traits.senses.note: Authored for a nocturnal rodent: high olfaction and vibration sensitivity for foraging in the dark, night vision, and no colour vision.

traits.social.note: 'Cape porcupines are nocturnal and monogamous, typically living as mated pairs of adults, caring for any young together.' The lower bound of 1 covers the individuals that forage alone, which the article also states.

traits.defense.note: The schema's enum has no quill category, and the article does not enumerate the responses of this species to a threat. Hide is recorded for the behaviour the article does document, retreating into a burrow among as many as six per pair, with the species' quills as the backstop; a reviewer who prefers Flee should change it.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from a large nocturnal herbivore that keeps to burrows by day and is described as a crop pest, i.e. habituated to open cleared ground but not to people.

habitat.use.note: Almost entirely terrestrial: it 'typically forages as individuals' on the ground, using burrows as shelter. The 0.95/0.5 split is authored from that, with only the small time spent in the burrow itself counted as fossorial.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'Each pair may inhabit up to six burrows, jointly defending their shared territory.'

habitat.resources.note: The four food tags map onto the diet sentence in the article; burrow appears twice, once for shelter and once for nesting, both from the same sourced sentence. Weights are authored.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: uses_gardens and Adapter are derived from 'they can feed on crops and damage trees' and are often considered pests by local farmers, which places the species in cultivated ground. impervious_max, dist_building_min_m, light_max and road_mortality are authored.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes no migration, dormancy or seasonal inactivity for this species, so ActiveYearRound is recorded by inference from the absence of any stated seasonal change.

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives no calendar window for breeding, so a single year-long territorial phase stands for the pair's year-round occupation of its burrows and territory. The label and the dates are authored.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'They are weaned at around 100 days of age' gives the juvenile duration. There is no egg stage in this schema's enum for a mammal, and the 0.55 scale is authored.

look.note: Authored, and explicitly a judgement rather than a sourced description: the article discusses diet and burrowing but gives no plumage or coat description, so the colours here follow the well-known appearance of the species - a dark brown, heavily built rodent with a short tail and a crown and rump of long pale-tipped quills. Proportions are authored. A reviewer wanting a sourced description should replace this block.

behavior.note: Mostly authored for the shared ground-forager program, which the article's behaviour supports: a nocturnal ground forager that walks out from a burrow to browse, and returns to shelter by day. The program description says the daytime rest window defaults suit nocturnal species, so the default 10 to 90 degrees is kept.
